content: Hellebores, commonly referred to as hellebores, are herbaceous perennial flowering plants belonging to the genus Helleborus. This genus consists of approximately 20 species, though ongoing research may alter this number. These plants are part of the family Ranunculaceae, within which they lend their name to the tribe Helleboreae. Many species within this genus are known to be toxic. The genus Helleborus is native to a wide range of Europe, extending from western Great Britain, Spain, and Portugal, across the Mediterranean region and central Europe, reaching as far as Romania and Ukraine. It also spans along the northern coast of Turkey into the Caucasus. The highest concentration of species is found in the Balkans. Two atypical species exist outside this range: Helleborus thibetanus, native to western China, and Helleborus vesicarius, which inhabits a small area on the border between Turkey and Syria. The flowers of hellebores are characterized by five petal-like structures, which are actually sepals or tepals, surrounding a ring of small, cup-shaped nectaries. These nectaries are modified petals designed to hold nectar. Unlike true petals, the sepals do not fall off but remain on the plant, sometimes for several months. Research conducted in Spain suggests that the persistent calyx contributes to seed development. Despite their resemblance to wild roses and common names like Christmas rose or Lenten rose, hellebores are not part of the rose family (Rosaceae). Species and Subspecies Caulescent Species These species have leaves on their flowering stems. In the case of Helleborus vesicarius, the stems die back annually, and the plant also has basal leaves. Examples include: Helleborus argutifolius (Corsican hellebore) Helleborus foetidus (Stinking hellebore or Setterwort) Helleborus lividus Helleborus vesicarius Acaulescent (Stemless) Species These species have basal leaves and lack true leaves on their flower stalks, though leafy bracts may be present where the flower stalks branch. Examples include: Helleborus atrorubens Helleborus croaticus Helleborus cyclophyllus Helleborus dumetorum Helleborus abruzzicus Helleborus liguricus Helleborus bocconei Helleborus multifidus (with subspecies such as H. multifidus subsp. hercegovinus, H. multifidus subsp. istriacus, and H. multifidus subsp. multifidus) Helleborus niger (Christmas rose or Black hellebore, with subspecies H. niger subsp. macranthus and H. niger subsp. niger) Helleborus odorus (with subspecies H. odorus subsp. laxus and H. odorus subsp. odorus) Helleborus orientalis (Lenten hellebore, with subspecies such as H. orientalis subsp. abchasicus, H. orientalis subsp. guttatus, and H. orientalis subsp. orientalis) Helleborus purpurascens Helleborus thibetanus (syn. H. chinensis) Helleborus torquatus Helleborus viridis (Green hellebore or Bear's-foot) Helleborus occidentalis (formerly H. viridis subsp. occidentalis) Some older species names, now considered invalid, may still appear in historical literature, such as H. hyemalis, H. polychromus, H. ranunculinus, and H. trifolius. Horticulture Hellebores are widely cultivated in gardens for their ornamental value, medicinal properties, and historical associations with witchcraft. They are particularly prized for their ability to bloom in winter and early spring, as well as their remarkable frost resistance. Many species are evergreen. Certain species, such as Helleborus argutifolius (Corsican hellebore), are popular for their pale green, cup-shaped flowers and attractive leathery foliage. Similarly, Helleborus foetidus (Stinking hellebore or Setterwort) is valued for its drooping clusters of small, pale green, bell-shaped flowers, often edged with maroon, which contrast beautifully with its dark evergreen foliage. Cultivars like H. foetidus 'Wester Flisk' with red-flushed flowers and stems, as well as selections with golden-yellow foliage, are gaining popularity. The Christmas rose (Helleborus niger) is a traditional favorite, producing pure white flowers that often age to pink during the depths of winter. Large-flowered cultivars, as well as pink-flowered and double-flowered selections, are available. However, the most popular hellebores for garden use are undoubtedly Helleborus orientalis and its colorful hybrids (H. × hybridus). These hybrids bloom in early spring, around Lent, and are often referred to as Lenten hellebores or Lenten roses. They are ideal for adding early color to shady herbaceous borders, areas beneath deciduous shrubs, and under trees. Hellebore Hybrids Hybridization, both deliberate and accidental, between H. orientalis and closely related species has significantly expanded the color range of hellebore flowers. These now include shades of slate grey, near-black, deep purple, plum, rich red, pink, yellow, white, and green. The outer surface of the sepals often has a green tinge, and as the flowers age, they typically become greener inside and out. Individual flowers can remain on the plant for a month or more. The inner surface of the sepals may feature veins, dots, or blotches in pink, red, or purple. Picotee flowers, with pale sepals edged in a darker color, are highly sought after, as are those with dark nectaries that contrast with the outer sepals. Recent breeding efforts have also produced double-flowered and anemone-centered plants. Double flowers have multiple rows of petals, while anemone-centered flowers feature a ring of shorter, curved extra petals (sometimes trumpet-shaped) within the five normal outer petals. These extra petals, often called petaloids, drop off after pollination, leaving what appears to be a single flower. Interspecific Hybrids Gardeners and nurserymen have also created hybrids between less closely related species. One of the earliest was H. × nigercors, a cross between H. niger and H. argutifolius, first made in 1931. H. × sternii, a cross between H. argutifolius and H. lividus, was first exhibited in 1947 and named after the British plantsman Sir Frederick Stern. Other hybrids, such as H. × ballardiae (H. niger crossed with H. lividus) and H. × ericsmithii (H. niger crossed with H. × sternii), honor British nursery owners Helen Ballard and Eric Smith. More recently, Ashwood Nurseries in England has developed hybrids like H. 'Pink Ice' (H. niger × H. thibetanus) and H. 'Briar Rose' (H. niger × H. vesicarius), though their garden worthiness remains to be proven. Folklore and Historical Usage In early medicine, two types of hellebore were recognized: black hellebore, which included various species of Helleborus, and white hellebore, now identified as Veratrum album (false hellebore). While Veratrum album is highly toxic, containing veratrine and teratogens like cyclopamine and jervine, it is believed to be the hellebore used by Hippocrates as a purgative. Black hellebore was historically used to treat paralysis, gout, and other diseases, particularly insanity. However, it is also toxic, causing symptoms such as tinnitus, vertigo, stupor, thirst, suffocation, swelling of the tongue and throat, vomiting, diarrhea, bradycardia, and ultimately collapse and death from cardiac arrest. Hellebores are surrounded by legends. In witchcraft, they are believed to have ties to summoning demons. Helleborus niger is commonly called the Christmas rose due to a legend that it sprouted in the snow from the tears of a young girl who had no gift to offer the Christ child in Bethlehem. In Greek mythology, Melampus of Pylos used hellebore to cure the daughters of the king of Argos from madness induced by Dionysus, which caused them to run naked through the city, crying and screaming. During the Siege of Kirrha in 585 BC, Greek besiegers reportedly used hellebore to poison the city's water supply, weakening the defenders with diarrhea and rendering them unable to defend the city. Some historians speculate that Alexander the Great may have died from a hellebore overdose, taken as medication.
